analysis.one_liner: Let economic cost-benefit tests and property-rights reviews override endangered species protections.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 Republican cosponsors, died in House committees without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the Endangered Species Act so that a species could no longer be listed as endangered or threatened based solely on the best available science — economic factors would count too. It would have barred any ESA action whose economic costs to society outweighed its benefits under a Reagan-era cost-benefit order. It also would have blocked every new federal regulation, from any agency, from taking effect until the Attorney General certified the agency was complying with a property-rights review order designed to minimize regulatory 'takings' of private property. The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main winners would be landowners and resource businesses — timber, mining, oil and gas, grazing, and real estate development — that face restrictions on how they can use land where a listed species lives. Removing 'solely' from the science-only listing standard and adding an economic cost-benefit gate would make it far harder to list species and impose those restrictions. The Attorney General certification requirement would also shield any industry from any new federal rule until its regulator passed a property-rights review.

how_it_helps.text: The bill deletes the word 'solely' from the ESA's requirement that listing decisions rest solely on the best scientific and commercial data available, opening listing decisions to non-scientific considerations.

It prohibits any action under the ESA unless potential economic benefits to society outweigh potential economic costs, as measured under Executive Order 12291, a cost-benefit framework from the Reagan administration.

It bars every new federal regulation from taking effect until the Attorney General certifies the issuing agency complies with Executive Order 12630, which requires agencies to assess whether a rule could take private property under the Fifth Amendment and to minimize such takings.

analysis.who_pays: The costs would fall on the public and on wildlife. Weakening the science-only listing standard and adding an economic veto would mean fewer species protected and fewer habitat restrictions, with the losses in extinction and ecosystem damage diffuse and long-term. The Attorney General certification requirement would also delay or stall the entire federal rulemaking process — clean air, workplace safety, everything — not just ESA rules, until each agency was certified.

drawbacks.text: The bill responds to a real grievance: under the ESA, landowners can be barred from using their own property to protect a species, bearing the full cost of a public good without compensation, and the bill's property-rights certification provision is aimed squarely at that problem.

But the remedy is far broader than the problem. The certification requirement covers every regulation from every executive agency, not just ESA rules, and the economic test could block listing a species even where the science is unambiguous — undoing the science-only standard Congress wrote into the ESA in 1973.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The property-rights concern behind the bill is genuine, and ESA restrictions can impose heavy, uncompensated burdens on individual landowners. But this bill's remedies are sweeping and poorly targeted: an economic cost-benefit gate on species listing, and a freeze on all federal rulemaking pending Attorney General certification, would hobble far more than the ESA and put protection decisions in the hands of economic and legal reviewers rather than scientists. A narrower landowner-compensation approach would have addressed the same grievance at far less cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to their subcommittees, the Interior Department's views were requested, and nothing further happened before the 103rd Congress ended, killing it.

narrative.text: Rep. James Hansen introduced the bill on March 18, 1993, joined by 17 original cosponsors, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Merchant Marine and Fisheries and on Judiciary.

Within two weeks it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Administrative Law and Governmental Relations and the Merchant Marine Subcommittee on Environment and Natural Resources, and executive comment was requested from the Interior Department.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Endangered Species Act's science-only listing standard and the normal federal rulemaking process stayed intact. The resource and development interests seeking easier land use did not get the changes they backed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Existing endangered species protections stayed intact

for.name: Rep. James V. Hansen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Human Protection Act of 1993 and gave introductory remarks on the floor.

for.name: 22 of 176 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Reps. Don Young of Alaska, Dick Armey of Texas, and Robert Smith of Oregon.

against.name: House Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee
against.role: Committee of primary jurisdiction over the Endangered Species Act
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Environment and Natural Resources Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral, sent it to its Administrative Law and Governmental Relations Subcommittee, and never brought it to a markup or vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 23 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans, and no vote was ever taken; the Democratic-majority committees simply never acted on the bill.

industries.industry: Logging, mining, and oil and gas interests
industries.note: These industries face some of the largest land-use restrictions under ESA listings, so an economic gate on listing and a science-only standard removed would directly free them from habitat constraints. The public would bear the cost in lost species protection.

industries.industry: Real estate developers and large private landowners
industries.note: ESA habitat restrictions can block or delay development on private land; the bill's economic test and property-rights certification requirement would ease both, while shifting the conservation burden onto the public.

The bill would freeze every new agency regulation until Attorney General certification of property-rights compliance, adding a layer of executive and judicial review over all rulemaking. Agencies would lose flexibility but gain a defined certification path.
